full_judgment:
2. Short facts for the purpose of disposal of this Rule are that the petitioner filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 156 of 1973 under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 for pre-empting 0.33 acres of land. His case was that present opposite party Nos. 6-11 were his co-sharers in the holding and opposite party No. 6 was his brother who secretly sold the land under pre-emption to one Surendra Nath Mistry in the benami of his wife Charubala Mistry and the opposite party No. 1 by two different kabalas dated 3.4.63 and 15.5.63 for a consideration of Tk. 600/- and Tk. 400/- respectively. It was further alleged by him that the purchasers were the strangers to the holding. It. was the further case of the petitioner that Surendra Nath Mistry and one Benode Behari got a Mcadipatta of the disputed land from opposite party No. 6 since May, 1962 and Surendra Nath was in possession but the opposite party No. 1 did not possess the disputed land and no statutory notices were served upon the petitioner. It was further alleged that after he came to know about the transfer from one Monoranjan and Nishi Kanta Howlader towards the end of Sravan, 1380 B.S. he made an enquiry and obtained certified copies of the kabalas on 15.11.73 when he came to know definitely about the transfer of the land under pre-emption. 

 6. It was urged that the lower appellate Court committed error of law on the face of record in holding that the application was not maintainable in view of provision of sub-rule 2 of rule 2 of Order 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner placed reliance upon the case of Hajee Majarullah Sowdager Vs. Mvi. Nurul Haque and others, 23 D.L.R. 68. Before considering that decision let me first consider the provisions of Order 2, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Sub-rule (1) of rule 2 provides that every suit shall include the whole of the claim which the plaintiff is entitled to make in respect of the cause of action, but a plaintiff may relinquish any portion of his claim in order to bring the suit within the jurisdiction of any court and sub-rule (2) provides where a plaintiff omits to sue in respect of or intentionally relinquishes, any portion of his claim, he shall not afterwards sue in respect of the portion as omitted or relinquished, Thus from reading the aforesaid provisions, it seems to me, that sub-rule 2 is no bar to an application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-empting lands transferred by more than one kabala on different dates. Rather, by reason of sub-rule 1 a petitioner is competent to include the whole of the claim which he is entitled to make in respect of the cause of action. In this respect it would be pertinent to refer to rule 3 of Order 2 as well which provides that "Save as otherwise provided, a plaintiff may unite in the same suit several causes of action against the same suit, several causes of action against the same defendant, or the same defendants jointly; and any plaintiff having causes of action in which they are jointly interested against the same defendant or the same defendants jointly may unite such cause of action in the same suit." Thus under rule 3 of Order 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure the petitioner was competent to initiate the present case by filing one application under section 96(1) of the Act wherein cause of action has been united. Now I proceed to examine as to whether there is any bar in the provisions of section 96 of the Act in filing of one application for pre-empting land transferred by different kabalas. From reading section 96 it seems to me that it enjoins that a petitioner to succeed in a pre-emption case must satisfy the requirements laid down in the section itself and non-compliance with those requirements of law will disentitle a pre-emptor from the right of pre-emption. But it is not the requirement of section 96 that a pre-emptor is to file separate application for each transfer or, in other words, by one application he is not entitled to pre-empt the lands transferred by different kabalas. A pre-emptor is certainly entitled to institute by a single application a proceeding under section 96(1) of the Act for pre-empting lands transferred by different kabalas on different dates provided the application is not otherwise barred by limitation and rule 2 of Order 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure is no bar to such an application and the pre-emptor is not required in law to seek leave of the Court for filing one application for pre-empting lands transferred by different kabalas on different dates. The lower appellate Court committed an error of law in holding that a single application was not maintainable in view of the provisions of rule 2 of Order 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The case re-ported in 23 DLR 68 also arose out of an application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-empting lands transferred by 3 sets of documents wherein it has been held that an applicant under section 96 can join several causes of action in one application arising out of several independent transfers or sales subject to the question of limitation and other conditions relating to maintainability of an application for pre-emption and jurisdiction of the court both pecuniary and territorial and if the cause of action arises from the date of knowledge of the sale which is the same in respect of all the sales in question then there can not be any difficulty in filing one application for pre-emption by the applicant inasmuch as the limitation runs from the same date and the Court has jurisdiction to entertain  the same.  The aforesaid observation necessitates an examination as to the question of limitation in this case. It was urged on behalf of the petitioner that the purchaser had been in possession of the land on the basis of a Meadipatta which was for ten years. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submitted that the said Meadipatta was for only 0.20 decimals of land, not for 0.33 decimals of land which was under pre-emption and, moreover, the patta land was also redeemed prior to transfer under pre-emption. Thus, according to him, the purchaser was not in possession of the land on the basis of patta and the pre-emptor had knowledge of the sale from the beginning. It appears that the appellate Court has considered the evidence led by both the parties in this respect and he came to the finding: "I am inclined to hold that really petitioner came to know of the kabalas from before and as a matter of fart, the story that he came to know of the two kabalas for the first time towards the end of Sravan, 1380, B.S. from Monoranjan and Nishi Kanta is a concocted one. This Miscellaneous Case, therefore, is hopelessly barred by limitation."
